lead: The first reading gives the law of the Jubilee. After seven times seven years, on the Day of Atonement, a trumpet sounds through the whole land, and the fiftieth year is holy: liberty is proclaimed, each family returns to its property, the land rests, and no one is to cheat a neighbour. In the Gospel, a different kind of power appears: Herod, who has imprisoned John the Baptist for telling him “It is not lawful for you to have her,” gives in to a dancing girl and her mother and has John beheaded. The jubilee is a year of release; Herod’s court is a place of fear and bondage, and John, in prison, is the one truly at liberty. The memorial of St Ignatius of Loyola, whose proper readings (1 Corinthians 10:31–11:1 and Luke 14:25–33) may be used instead, is kept today.

r.h: You shall return, every one of you, to your property
set: Leviticus 25 is part of the Holiness Code. It begins with the sabbatical year, in which the land rests every seventh year (25:1–7), and then gives the law of the Jubilee: after seven sabbaths of years, forty-nine years, the fiftieth year is a year of release. The word “Sinai” in verse 1 recalls that these are laws given by God to Israel at the mountain.

The law rests on the conviction that the land belongs to God (25:23): Israel’s families are tenants and stewards, not absolute owners. If poverty forced a family to sell its land or itself into service, the jubilee returned them to their inheritance. Scholars debate how fully the jubilee was kept in ancient Israel, but the prophets and the Gospels hold it up as an ideal of what God wants.
str: v. 1: the Lord speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai.
vv. 8–9: seven weeks of years; on the Day of Atonement the trumpet sounds throughout the land.
vv. 10–12: the fiftieth year is holy; liberty is proclaimed; each returns to his property and family; the land is not sown.
v. 13: “you shall return, every one of you, to your property”.
vv. 14–17: honest dealing: prices fixed by the number of harvests until the next jubilee; “you shall not cheat one another, but you shall fear your God”.
kw: Originally the ram’s horn that was blown to announce the year. The Latin iubilaeum, “jubilee”, comes from it, though it later came to be associated with iubilare, “to rejoice”.
The word for the freedom proclaimed in the year of jubilee, found again in Isaiah 61:1 and Jeremiah 34:8. Jesus quotes the Isaiah text in the synagogue of Nazareth (Luke 4:18).
From the verb yānâ, “to oppress, to wrong”, used in verses 14 and 17 (“you shall not cheat one another”). The jubilee law forbids it, and verse 17 grounds the prohibition in the fear of God.
vv: you shall proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants.

The liberty is for all the inhabitants of the land. These words were later carved on the Liberty Bell in Philadelphia, but their first meaning is the release of the poor and the return of families to their land.
you shall return, every one of you, to your property and every one of you to your family.
Property and family go together. The jubilee guards both the means of life and the bond of kinship, so that no family is cut off for ever.
you shall eat only what the field itself produces.
The year of rest is a year of trust. The land is not worked, and the people depend on what God gives without their labour.
You shall not cheat one another, but you shall fear your God;
The law of the market is joined to the fear of God. Honest dealing is not only a matter of law but of reverence for the Lord who sees.
ch: The Church reads the jubilee in the light of Jesus’ first sermon at Nazareth, where he reads from Isaiah 61, “to proclaim release to the captives… to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor,” and says that it is fulfilled today (Luke 4:16–21). Since 1300 the Church has also celebrated Holy Years, as times of pilgrimage, conversion and mercy; Pope John Paul II linked them expressly with Leviticus 25 (Tertio Millennio Adveniente 11–13). The Catechism teaches the universal destination of goods: God gave the earth to the whole human race, and private property does not remove the claim of the poor on what is superfluous (CCC 2402–2403). The jubilee is a standing reminder that every possession is held in trust.

r.h: Herod sent and had John beheaded in the prison
set: The account follows the rejection of Jesus at Nazareth. Herod “the ruler” is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who governed Galilee and Perea as tetrarch from 4 BC until AD 39. Matthew has just told that Jesus’ fame was spreading, and now Herod hears of it and fears that John the Baptist, whom he killed, has been raised.

The story is a flashback: Matthew tells how John came to die. Herod had married Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip; John said that this was not lawful, as the Law of Moses forbids a man to marry his brother’s wife while the brother is alive (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21). Matthew’s account is brief; the historian Josephus also tells of John’s death and says that Herod put him to death at the fortress of Machaerus.
str: vv. 1–2: Herod hears of Jesus and thinks he is John raised from the dead.
vv. 3–5: the flashback: John imprisoned for saying “It is not lawful”; Herod wants to kill him but fears the crowd.
vv. 6–11: Herod’s birthday, the dance, the oath, the request for John’s head, and the beheading.
v. 12: John’s disciples bury him and tell Jesus.
kw: Literally “ruler of a fourth part”. Matthew calls Herod “the ruler”, and in v. 9 “the king”, as he was called by courtesy though Rome had not given him the title.
Herod binds himself by an oath, and the oath becomes his excuse. Jesus teaches elsewhere that his disciples should not swear at all (Matthew 5:33–37), and this story shows why.
A flat dish for food. The head on a platter is the grim reversal of a banquet, where the guests are fed and a prophet is killed.
vv: It is not lawful for you to have her.
John is not afraid of a king. He speaks the truth about marriage and the Law and he pays for it. The same word “lawful” is used of the Sabbath and divorce elsewhere in Matthew.
Though Herod wanted to put him to death, he feared the crowd,
Herod’s fear of the crowd restrains him for a while. Later, fear of the guests and of his own oath moves him in the other direction. A man who fears people and not God can be led anywhere.
The king was grieved, yet out of regard for his oaths and for the guests, he commanded it to be given;
The most tragic line of the story: he is sorry, and he does it. Regret that does not turn into action is no protection.
His disciples came and took the body and buried it; then they went and told Jesus.
The disciples of John give him a burial and take the news to Jesus. With this, John’s story passes into Jesus’ story: the forerunner’s death foreshadows his own (Matthew 17:12).
ch: The Church honours John the Baptist as the forerunner who prepared the way, and as a martyr for the truth: his death is kept on 29 August as the Passion of St John the Baptist. The Catechism teaches that martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith (CCC 2473), and it presents John as the one who goes before the Lord “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (CCC 523). His death is a sign for every Christian who speaks the truth where it is unwelcome. Herod’s story is the other side: one who knew John was a holy man (Mark 6:20) and still chose to protect his own position.

rite: St Ignatius of Loyola (1491–1556) was born into a Basque noble family. As a soldier he was wounded at Pamplona in 1521, and while he recovered at Loyola he read the lives of Christ and the saints, and his life turned. After a year of prayer at Manresa he wrote the first notes of the Spiritual Exercises, a month of guided prayer that has shaped countless lives. In 1540 Pope Paul III approved his Society of Jesus. Its motto, “for the greater glory of God”, is the thread of the proper readings: “whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31) and the cost of following Christ (Luke 14:25–33). He died in Rome on 31 July 1556 and was canonised in 1622.
study: The jubilee returns each family to its land and each person to freedom. Is there a debt, a grievance or an old wrong that I can release this week?
Herod grieved, and yet obeyed his oath and his guests. When have I done something I knew to be wrong because of what others would think, and what would have helped me to stand firm?
